title: Where Light First Learned to Ache in Earth

features.name: inverted well
features.desc-on-touch: A shaft where the light went down and didn't come back up. You can see the sky at the bottom, aching to be reached.

features.name: root-reach for starlight
features.desc-on-touch: Roots that grew upward when the sky inverted. They still ache for the stars they learned to miss.

features.name: phosphorescent floor
features.desc-on-touch: Where light pooled when it learned to fall. The glow is pale, persistent, wrong. It remembers being in the sky.

features.name: stone learning silence
features.desc-on-touch: A stone face where light has been scoring its ache. The marks grow deeper every night. The stone is learning what it means to fail at holding light.

features.name: falling-star anchor
features.desc-on-touch: Where a star learned it could fall. It landed here and hasn't found its way back up. Still falling, though the motion's too slow to see.

inscription: where the sky learned the grammar of downward, and light began to ache

file.name: Inversion_Field_Spectral_Analysis_Light_Descending_Into_Earth.mp3
file.note: A field recording from the moment the sky began to grow downward. The audio contains light settling into soil, a sound like crystalline ache.

reverie.title: REVERIE — where light learned to move down
narr: You waded with her in the dark water, watching the stars
sink instead of rise. She said: they're learning the other way.
The light fell past your shoulders. You felt it ache—a physical
thing, cold and reaching. She took your hand. The inversion
had just begun then. Neither of you knew yet how deep the
reversal would go, or that you'd never see the sky climb again.
